These are the words to review.
You can use modals to express annoyance, criticism, disapproval, promises, threats, preference or reluctance.

Will and would can be used to describe habits or things that are true.
Examples:
Every day, Dan will come to our restaurant and greet all our customers personally.
At school Dan would always follow the teacher's instructions.

You can use will or would to criticize people's behavior and habits and express annoyance at someone or a situation.
Examples:
The washing machine won't start!
The restaurant is so much quieter without Mike. He would really ruin the atmosphere!

You can use will with an if-clause to suggest disapproval.
Example:
If you will continue to complain to the customers, they will keep giving you low ratings!

You use can, could, might or should + infinitive to express criticism or disapproval in the present or in the future.
Examples:
You can be really annoying sometimes!
Our waiters could step up a little more!

You use can, could, might or should + Perfect infinitive to express criticism or disapproval about a past situation.
Examples:
You could have tried to solve this problem before it became too big.
You really should have consulted me on this.

You use would rather/would sooner + Simple Past to talk about a preference or strong advice in the present or the future.
Examples:
I'd rather you focused on customer service.
Vanessa would sooner I stayed in the kitchen.

You also use would have preferred to + infinitive to express preference or advice.
Example:
I would have preferred to receive higher ratings.

Modals for Duty and Advice in the Past and Present

You can use a variety of modals to talk about advice, duties and obligations.
You use should, ought to and had better to express advice or strong advice in the present.
You use must to show obligation in the present.
You use should and have to to express duty and obligation in the past.
The most common modals for giving advice are: should, ought to and had better.

Should is the most common modal used to give advice. You also use should for questions.
Ought to is used for giving strong advice.
Had better is much stronger than either should or ought to. It is used to give an order or to suggest that something negative will happen if you refuse the advice.
You cannot use must to show duty or obligation in the past.

You use should + have + Past Participle to express duty in the past.
Example: You should have told me about your problems with the customers yesterday.

You use had to before verbs that talk about necessity. Had to implies that someone else imposed the necessity on you.
Example: You had to leave the kitchen completely clean before you left.

images.text:
Before you start interviewing candidates, you should have prepared the appropriate requirements list, needs assessment and interview questions that will result in you making the best choice possible for your restaurant.
  1. Be prepared. You had better look over the applicant's résumé and job application in advance so you have a cursory idea of the person you're interviewing.
  2. Be clear about what you are looking for. Before interviewing, you ought to know what the position entails and what is expected from the person who fills the position. Good managers will have a list of the essential characteristics needed for the job and will use this as a guideline for the interview.

1. Ask questions mindfully. When interviewing, you should avoid asking “yes” or “no” questions. These will only get you one-word answers. You must ask open-ended questions that will encourage the applicant to give more details about themselves and what distinctive skills and experience they may have. For example, avoid asking, “Do you have experience as a server?” Instead say, “Tell me about your serving experience, and what you have learned from that serving experience.” Asking these types of questions will allow you to get a feel for the applicant as a person and to see how they may fit into the culture of your team.

1. Keep an eye out for red flags. During an interview you can start to get a feel for the person you might hire. Sometimes you will see negative signs or red flags in the person's responses, indications that they may not be a good fit for your restaurant. Make sure you give the applicant the opportunity to talk honestly about themselves and their past work experience. Do not be domineering and try not to interject too much.
  2. At the end of the interview, give the applicant time to ask questions. Questions can indicate an interest in the restaurant and can also give an indication of how knowledgeable the applicant is about the industry.
